plot: Odo and Mothwick follow the medieval record of the Green Children of Woolpit: reapers find a green-skinned brother and sister by the wolf pits who speak an unknown language and eat only raw beans; the boy dies, the girl Agnes loses her green colour and describes a sunless twilight land; the twist (clue planted early: they were starving) is that they were probably lost Flemish orphans turned green by hunger, and Agnes lives on and marries.

beats.say: 1150s, Woolpit, England. Two children climbed out of a wolf pit. Green.
Green? Like moss green? Mothwick, children aren't green.
Harvest time. Reapers in the field saw them by the wolf pits.
Two old monks wrote this down, Odo. Separately. It is history.
A brother and a sister. Their skin was green all over.
Their clothes were made of a cloth nobody had seen before.
Where are you from? Who is your father? Can you hear me?
They answered in a language no one in Suffolk knew.
Maybe they were just lost? Somebody must have missed them.
The reapers took them to the house of Sir Richard de Calne.
Bring them bread. Meat. Milk. They must be starving.
They would not eat. Not bread, not meat. For days.
Not even honey? Children, please. You will not last a week.
Remember this, Odo. Starving. For days. Before they were found too.
Then they saw raw beans still on the stalks, and grabbed them.
For months, they ate nothing but beans.
Beans? That's the strangest food to choose. Why beans?
The boy grew weaker and weaker. Soon after he was baptised, he died.
But the girl lived. And here is where it gets stranger.
Subscribe for a new true story every day. Now, her answer.
Slowly she ate other food. And her skin lost its green.
She learned English. She was named Agnes. Then they asked her.
In our land, the sun never rises. It is always twilight.
Everyone there is green. Across a wide river, we saw a bright land.
We followed our father's cattle into a cave. We heard bells.
We walked toward the bells. Then we were in your field.
A land with no sun? Mothwick, she came from underground?
That's what people believed for eight hundred years.
William of Newburgh and Ralph of Coggeshall both wrote it down.
Ralph said Sir Richard himself told him, many times.
So who were they really? Please don't say fairies.
Here is one answer historians give. Remember the starving.
England was at war with itself. Flemish families were driven out.
Near Woolpit was Fordham St Martin, a village with a river.
Flemish children would speak a language nobody here knew.
Lost in thick forest, they might never see open sun.
And starving children can turn a sickly green. It's called chlorosis.
So the green wasn't magic. It was hunger. That's worse.
Nobody can prove it. The church bells of Bury may have led them.
Agnes worked in Sir Richard's house for many years.
Ralph says she married a man at King's Lynn.
Today the village sign of Woolpit shows the two green children.
I'm eating all my supper tonight. Even the beans.
If this one got you, the Christmas ghost army of Edgehill is next.
Have you heard a story like this one? Tell me in the comments.

long.title: Legend of Woolpit: 2 Green Children Appeared | True Story
long.description:
Previous true story: https://youtu.be/1ntmNRGVkKg
Have you heard a story like this one? Tell me in the comments.

"They wouldn't eat bread. Only raw beans. And their skin was green." — Odo

A true record from 12th-century Suffolk: at harvest time, reapers in Woolpit found a brother and sister with green skin by the wolf pits, speaking an unknown language and refusing all food but raw beans. The boy died; the girl, Agnes, lost her green colour, learned English and told of a twilight land. Two medieval chroniclers, William of Newburgh and Ralph of Coggeshall, wrote it down.

Sources:
